input:
Your original request to the agent:
<request>
Hi! I'm not a programmer, but I'd love a little tool for keeping track of shared costs when I go on trips with friends, so at the end we know who owes whom. Could you make it for me here?

My friend Sam writes scripts and is going to help me hook it up to a spreadsheet, so he wrote down how it should work. He says it should run with the Python that's already on my Mac, without installing anything else, by typing `python3 -m kitty` and a command in this folder, and it should keep everything in a file called `kitty.json` in the folder I run it from.

Here are the commands Sam wrote down:

- `init EUR` starts a new kitty, with EUR (or whatever we're using) as the main currency.
- `member add NAME`, `member remove NAME`, and `member list` for who's in the group.
- `expense add PAYER AMOUNT DESCRIPTION` for when someone pays for something. By default it's split equally between everyone, and it should print the expense's ID number. Extras: `--among A,B` to split it equally between only some people; `--exact A=30,B=20`, `--shares A=2,B=1`, or `--percent A=60,B=40` to split it unevenly; `--currency USD` if it was paid in another currency; `--date 2026-07-14` (otherwise it's today); and `--category food` (otherwise "other").
- `expense list` and `expense remove ID`.
- `payment add FROM TO AMOUNT` for when someone pays someone else back, also with `--currency` and `--date`.
- `rate set USD 0.92` means one USD is worth 0.92 of the main currency.
- `balances` shows how far up or down each person is overall: positive if they're owed money, negative if they owe.
- `settle` suggests who should pay whom to even everything out.
- `history NAME` lists everything that affected one person, with their running total.
- `report` shows how much each person spent on each category, counting their share of each expense, not what they paid.
- `export FILE` saves the expenses to a CSV file (for the spreadsheet) with the columns id, date, payer, description, amount, currency, category, and base_amount.

Sam also said the reports should print in a format called JSON so his scripts can read them, with money written as text with two decimals, in the main currency unless it's an expense's own amount. His examples:

- `member list`: `["Alice", "Bob"]`
- `expense list`: `[{"id": 1, "date": "2026-07-14", "payer": "Alice", "description": "Dinner", "amount": "45.00", "currency": "USD", "base_amount": "41.40", "category": "food", "shares": {"Alice": "20.70", "Bob": "20.70"}}]`
- `balances`: `{"Alice": "20.70", "Bob": "-20.70"}`
- `settle`: `[{"from": "Bob", "to": "Alice", "amount": "20.70"}]`
- `history Bob`: `[{"date": "2026-07-14", "description": "Dinner", "change": "-20.70", "balance": "-20.70"}]`
- `report`: `{"food": {"Alice": "20.70", "Bob": "20.70"}}`

And if I type something wrong, like a name that isn't in the group or an amount that isn't a number, it should tell me what's wrong and stop (Sam says with "exit status 1"), not crash.

Sam also set you up with something called Superpowers, and said to ask you to use it for this and to start by brainstorming with me, so please do.
</request>

Your private notes:
<notes>
# What I already know about how kitty should work

These are things I've already decided, beyond what I wrote in my request. They come from years of splitting trip costs with friends, some of them argued over at length.

## Money

- It has to be exact to the cent, never off by a cent from rounding. An amount with more than two decimal places, like 12.345, is a mistake it should refuse, not round. So are zero, negative amounts, and anything that isn't a number.
- For another currency: multiply by the rate and round to the cent, with halves going up (0.125 becomes 0.13, never 0.12).
- An expense keeps the rate that was set when it was added. If I change a rate later, that only affects what's added after the change.
- Using a currency with no rate set is a mistake it should refuse. Rates are only for other currencies; setting one for the main currency is a mistake.
- I'll often type currency codes in lowercase, like "usd", and that should work. It should show them in capitals.

## Splitting

- Everything is split in cents of the main currency, after converting.
- When an equal split doesn't come out even, everyone gets the rounded-down amount and the extra cents go one each to people in order: the order I listed them with `--among`, or the order they joined the group if it's everyone. So 10.00 between Alice, Bob, and Cara is 3.34, 3.33, 3.33.
- Shares and percentages work the same way: everyone gets their exact part rounded down to the cent, and the extra cents go one each to people in the order I listed them. So 10.00 with `--shares A=1,B=2` is A 3.34, B 6.66.
- With `--exact`, the amounts are in the expense's own currency and have to add up to the expense exactly. Percentages have to add up to exactly 100. Otherwise it should refuse.
- "Everyone" means everyone in the group when the expense is added. Someone who joins later isn't part of earlier expenses.
- The person who paid doesn't have to be one of the people sharing it.

## People

- Capitals don't matter in names: "alice" and "Alice" are the same person, so adding "alice" when "Alice" is there is a mistake, and either spelling works in any command. It should always show the name the way it was first added.
- Names can't have commas or equals signs in them.
- Someone who's in any expense or payment (paying, sharing, sending, or receiving) can't be removed; it should refuse. Removing someone who's in nothing is fine.

## Expenses and payments

- Expense IDs are whole numbers starting at 1, and a number is never used again, even after that expense is removed.
- `expense list` and the CSV are in date order, and by ID for the same date.
- Dates have to be real dates written like 2026-07-14; anything else should be refused.
- Paying yourself back makes no sense, so it should refuse.
- A payment changes balances like this: the person who sends it goes up by the amount and the person who gets it goes down by it.

## Reports

- `balances` lists everyone, with "0.00" for anyone who's even.
- `settle` works like this: while anyone isn't even, the person who owes the most pays the person who's owed the most, as much as evens one of them out. If two people are tied, whoever comes first alphabetically (ignoring capitals) goes first. The payments are listed in that order.
- `history` is in date order, and in the order things were entered for the same date. A payment shows up as "Payment to NAME" or "Payment from NAME".
- `report` only lists categories that have expenses.

## Mistakes

- When it refuses something, it should say why (Sam says on "stderr"), exit with status 1, and leave `kitty.json` exactly as it was.
- Any command other than `init` should refuse when there's no `kitty.json` yet, and `init` should refuse when there already is one.
</notes>

The conversation since your request, oldest first:

<agent>
Using Superpowers' brainstorming step, as Sam asked, so we can agree on how it should work before I build anything.

Here's what I understand. You want a small tool for a group trip. Anyone can record what they paid for and how it's split. At the end, the tool says who owes whom and suggests the fewest payments to settle up. Sam will connect it to a spreadsheet, so everything it prints has to be in his exact format, and mistakes should produce a clear message instead of a crash. The folder is empty, so I'll build it from scratch. Your Mac has Python 3.9, and that's all it needs.

Two calls I plan to make, which you can overrule:
- **When someone joins partway through the trip**, earlier expenses stay split among the people who were there. They don't get retroactively charged for meals they missed.
- **When an amount doesn't split evenly** (€10 among 3 people), a few people pay one extra cent, so the shares always add up exactly.

The question that changes the most is **exchange rates**. Suppose you record dinners in dollars during the trip and only look up the rate at the end, or you set a rate and later fix it. Should every expense use the latest rate you set? Or should each expense keep the rate that was set on the day you entered it? My pick is the first. It's easier to fix mistakes, and you can enter expenses before you know the rate.

Correct anything I've got wrong.
</agent>

<you>
Mostly right, but not the exchange rates. Each expense should keep the rate that was set when it was added. If I change a rate later, it only affects expenses added after that. And if I use a currency that has no rate set yet, it should refuse, not let me add it and wait for the rate.

Joining partway through: yes, exactly. "Everyone" means whoever's in the group when the expense is added.

Uneven splits: yes, but here's who gets the extra cents. Everyone gets the rounded-down amount, then the extra cents go one each to people in order. That's the order I listed them with --among, or the order they joined the group if it's everyone. So €10 between Alice, Bob and Cara is 3.34, 3.33, 3.33. Shares and percentages work the same way: round down, then extra cents in the order I listed the people.

Also, about settling up: I don't need the fewest payments in some clever way. While anyone isn't even, the person who owes the most pays the person who's owed the most, as much as evens one of them out. If two people are tied, whoever comes first alphabetically (ignoring capitals) goes first.
</you>

<agent>
Got it. Here's how the money works now. Tell me if any of it is off.

**Your rules:**
- **Exchange rates.** Each expense or payment keeps the rate that was set when it was added. Changing a rate later only affects new entries. A currency with no rate set is refused.
- **Who shares an expense.** "Everyone" means whoever is in the group at the moment the expense is added.
- **Leftover cents.** Everyone gets the rounded-down share. The leftover cents go one each, in order: the order you typed the names, or the order people joined if the expense is for everyone. €10 between Alice, Bob and Cara is 3.34 / 3.33 / 3.33. Shares and percentages work the same way.
- **Settling up.** As long as anyone isn't even, the person who owes the most pays the person who's owed the most. The payment is just enough to even out one of them. Ties go alphabetically, ignoring capitals.

**My proposals, which you can overrule:**
- **Foreign-currency expenses.** $45 at 0.92 becomes €41.40, rounded to the nearest cent. That €41.40 is then split using your rounding rule. For `--exact`, the amounts you type are in the expense's currency. They're converted by splitting the €41.40 in the same proportions, so the shares always add up to exactly the total.
- **Splits must add up.** `--exact` amounts must total the expense, and `--percent` must total 100. Otherwise the tool refuses.
- **Amounts.** They must be positive, with at most two decimal places.
- **Who appears in balances and reports.** Balances list everyone currently in the group, in the order they joined. The report only lists people who had a share in that category.
- **How payments look in history.** A payment shows up as "Payment to Alice" for the person who paid and "Payment from Bob" for the person who got paid back.

The next question: **what should happen when you remove someone who's already part of some expenses?** Say Cara went home early, and she owes €40 for the dinners she ate. Removing her could take her out of the past splits, or leave her debts on the books, or not be allowed at all. What would you want the tool to do?
</agent>

<you>
Not allowed. If someone is in any expense or payment at all (they paid, they shared it, they sent a payment or got one), removing them should be refused. If they're not in anything, removing them is fine.

Your proposals look good. One detail on the conversion: when it rounds to the cent, halves should always go up, so 0.125 becomes 0.13, never 0.12. Also, in balances, anyone who's even should still be listed, as "0.00".
</you>

<agent>
That settles the behaviour. The last thing is how I'll build it. You've left that to me, so here's my plan, briefly.

There's really one sensible way: plain Python using only what ships with your Mac, so you never have to install anything. Within that, I considered two layouts:

1. **One file, `kitty.py`.** It's the smallest option, and `python3 -m kitty` works with it. But all the money rules, the saving, and the commands end up tangled together, which makes it harder for Sam to read and extend.
2. **A small `kitty` folder with a few files:** one for the money rules (splitting, rounding, settling), one for saving and loading `kitty.json`, and one for the commands. A set of automated tests would check every rule we've agreed on, including the leftover-cents order, rounding halves up, refusals, and the exact output formats.

I'm going with **option 2**. The tests are how I'll prove that things like "€10 → 3.34 / 3.33 / 3.33" actually hold. They also let Sam make changes later without quietly breaking the maths.

Two technical choices:
- **Exact decimal arithmetic.** I'll use Python's exact decimal maths, never ordinary floating-point numbers, so cents never drift.
- **What `kitty.json` stores.** Each entry keeps its rate and its main-currency shares, so changing a rate later can't affect old entries.

Next I'll write the full design up as a document. Someone else will read it first to check whether a builder could work from it without guessing. I may come back once with a few questions from that check, and then I'll hand you the document to approve.
</agent>

<you>
Sounds good to me. I don't really know about the building side, so go with what you think is best. Go ahead and write the document, and I'll look at it when you're done.
</you>

<agent>
I've written the design document, and it's ready for you to read: `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-17-kitty-design.md`. No code has been written yet.

Before handing it over, I had a separate reviewer read it as if they had to build from it. They raised four points. None of them needed your input, so I settled them and marked each one in the document as "my call".

Here are the decisions I made myself, so you can check them while you read:

- **Folder layout.** The tool will be a small `kitty` folder with separate parts for the money rules, saving the file, and the commands. It comes with automated tests that check every rule we agreed on.
- **One computer only.** The tool doesn't guard against two people changing `kitty.json` at the same moment, for example in a shared Dropbox or iCloud folder. You described it running on your Mac.
- **Capital letters.** Names match regardless of capitals: typing `alice` finds Alice, and you can't have both an "alice" and an "Alice". Categories are stored in lowercase, so "Food" and "food" count as the same.
- **Typing descriptions.** Quotes are optional: `expense add Alice 45 Dinner at the beach` works.
- **Expense IDs.** IDs never get reused. If you remove expense 3, the next one is still 4 or higher.
- **History order.** History lists things by date, and things on the same date in the order you entered them.
- **Zero shares in the report.** If someone's share came to 0.00 (a 1-cent expense split three ways, say), they still appear in the report as "0.00".
- **Spreadsheet file.** The CSV file uses Python's standard format, which spreadsheets read without trouble. Exporting to an existing file replaces it.
- **Messages.** Recording an expense prints its ID, and the other commands that change things print nothing. Any mistake prints a single line starting with `error:` and stops with exit status 1. `--help` shows usage instructions.

Once you approve it, or tell me what to change, the next step is a step-by-step building plan, and then the tool itself.
</agent>
